etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English serchen, borrowed from Anglo-Norman sercher, Old French cerchier, from Late Latin circō, circāre (“to circle; go around; search for”), from Latin circa, circus. Not related to German suchen, which is cognate with English seek.

quote.citation: 2012 October 31, David M. Halbfinger, New York Times, retrieved 31 October 2012:
quote.text: At least eight people died, and officials expressed deep concerns that the toll would rise as more searches of homes were carried out.

definitions.definition: The act of searching in general.

quote.citation: 2013 June 14, Jonathan Freedland, “Obama's once hip brand is now tainted”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 189, number 1, page 18:
quote.text: Where we once sent love letters in a sealed envelope, or stuck photographs of our children in a family album, now such private material is despatched to servers and clouds operated by people we don't know and will never meet. Perhaps we assume that our name, address and search preferences will be viewed by some unseen pair of corporate eyes, probably not human, and don't mind that much.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To look in (a place) for something.

quote.citation: 1689 (indicated as 1690), [John Locke], An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding. […], London:  […]  Eliz[abeth] Holt, for Thomas Basset, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: It sufficeth that they have once with care and fairness sifted the matter as far as they could, and searched into all the particulars.

quote.citation: 1909, Archibald Marshall [pseudonym; Arthur Hammond Marshall], chapter I, in The Squire’s Daughter, New York, N.Y.: Dodd, Mead and Company, published 1919, →OCLC:
quote.text: He tried to persuade Cicely to stay away from the ball-room for a fourth dance. […] But she said she must go back, and when they joined the crowd again […] she found her mother standing up before the seat on which she had sat all the evening searching anxiously for her with her eyes, and her father by her side.

quote.citation: 2013 July 6, “The rise of smart beta”, in The Economist, volume 408, number 8843, page 68:
quote.text: Investors face a quandary. Cash offers a return of virtually zero in many developed countries; government-bond yields may have risen in recent weeks but they are still unattractive. Equities have suffered two big bear markets since 2000 and are wobbling again. It is hardly surprising that pension funds, insurers and endowments are searching for new sources of return.

definitions.definition: (transitive, now rare) To look for, seek.

quote.text: To search the God of loue, her Nymphes she sent / Throughout the wandring forrest euery where […].

quote.text: For thus saith the Lord God; Behold, I, even I, will both search my sheep, and seek them out.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book VII”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: Anough is left besides to search and know.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To put a phrase into a  search engine, especially one besides  Google.
(transitive, obsolete) To probe or examine (a wound).

quote.citation: 1485, Sir Thomas Malory, “xvj”, in Le Morte Darthur, book I:
quote.text: Now torne we to the xj kynges that retorned vnto a cyte that hyghte Sorhaute / the whiche cyte was within kynge Vryens / and ther they refresshed hem as wel as they myght / and made leches serche theyr woundys and sorowed gretely for the dethe of her peple(please add an English translation of this quotation)

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To examine; to try; to put to the test.
